decks.title: Sound — Part 1: Echoes and their uses
goals: Explain an echo and state the conditions for hearing a distinct echo
Justify the minimum distance of about 17 m for an echo in air
Calculate the speed of sound or the distance of a reflector from echo times
Explain how bats, dolphins, fishing boats, doctors and SONAR use echoes

slides.heading: Hello… hello… hello!
slides.body_md: Part 1 — shout towards a hill or a tall building and the sound comes back. Bats, dolphins, ships and doctors all use this returning sound.

rows: Your shout comes back a moment later

visual.alt: Table of four situations in which sound is reflected

slides.narration: Namaste! Stand in a valley and shout your name. A moment later you hear it again, coming back from the hills. That returning sound is an echo. In this part we find out when an echo can be heard, how to calculate distances from echo times, and how bats, dolphins, ships and doctors use echoes.

slides.heading: Reflection of sound and the echo
slides.body_md:
Sound is reflected from hard, large surfaces such as walls, cliffs and buildings, obeying the same laws of reflection as light. An **echo** is the sound heard **after reflection** from a distant obstacle, **separately** from the original sound. The sound travels to the reflector and back, a distance $2d$, so
$$d = \frac{v t}{2}, \qquad v = \frac{2d}{t}$$
where $t$ is the time between producing the sound and hearing the echo.

slides.narration: Sound bounces off hard surfaces just as light bounces off a mirror. When the reflected sound reaches us clearly after the original sound, we hear an echo. In the time we wait, the sound has gone to the cliff and come back, covering twice the distance. So the distance to the cliff is half of speed times time.

slides.heading: Conditions for hearing a distinct echo
slides.body_md:
1. **Time gap:** the sensation of a sound lasts in our ear for about **0.1 s** (persistence of hearing). The echo must arrive **at least 0.1 s** after the original sound to be heard separately.
2. **Minimum distance:** in 0.1 s sound in air (about 340 m/s) travels $340 \times 0.1 = 34$ m, there and back, so the reflector must be at least **17 m** away.
3. **Size of reflector:** the reflecting surface must be **large** compared with the wavelength of the sound.
4. **Loudness:** the sound must be **loud enough** for the echo to be heard.

nodes.label: Ear holds a sound for 0.1 s
Round trip must take at least 0.1 s

visual.alt: Flow from persistence of hearing to the minimum distance of seventeen metres

slides.narration: Our ears hold on to each sound for about one tenth of a second. If the reflected sound comes back sooner, it merges with the original and we cannot hear it separately. In one tenth of a second, sound in air travels about thirty four metres. That is there and back, so the reflector must be at least seventeen metres away. It must also be large, and the sound loud.

slides.heading: Worked example: minimum distance on a warm day
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** On a warm afternoon the speed of sound in air is 344 m/s. Find the minimum distance of a wall from a person for a distinct echo to be heard.

**Given:** $t = 0.1$ s (persistence of hearing), $v = 344$ m/s.

**Distance:** $d = \dfrac{v t}{2} = \dfrac{344 \times 0.1}{2} = 17.2$ m.

So the wall must be at least about 17.2 m away.

visual.alt: Table of the values in the minimum distance example

slides.narration: The echo must arrive at least a tenth of a second after the sound. In that time sound at three hundred and forty four metres per second covers thirty four point four metres. Half of that, seventeen point two metres, is the least distance of the wall. On a warmer day sound is faster, so this distance is slightly larger.

slides.heading: Quick check: minimum distance
slides.body_md: Find the least distance for a distinct echo.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use one tenth of a second, and remember that the sound goes there and back.

slides.heading: Worked example: clapping near a building
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Farhan claps once in front of a tall building and hears the echo 1.2 s later. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. (a) How far is the building? (b) If he walks 68 m closer, after what time will he hear the echo?

**(a)** $d = \dfrac{v t}{2} = \dfrac{340 \times 1.2}{2} = 204$ m.

**(b)** New distance $= 204 - 68 = 136$ m; $t = \dfrac{2d}{v} = \dfrac{2 \times 136}{340} = 0.8$ s.

visual.alt: Table of distance and echo time before and after walking closer

slides.narration: Sound covers three hundred and forty times one point two, or four hundred and eight metres, there and back, so the building is two hundred and four metres away. After walking sixty eight metres closer, he is one hundred and thirty six metres away. The round trip is now two hundred and seventy two metres, which takes point eight seconds.

slides.heading: Quick check: echo time
slides.body_md: Find the time after which an echo is heard.
slides.narration: Quick check. Time equals twice the distance divided by the speed of sound.

slides.heading: Echoes in nature and medicine
slides.body_md:
Many uses of echoes need **ultrasound** — sound of frequency **above 20 kHz**, beyond human hearing. Ultrasound has a **short wavelength**, so it travels in a narrow beam and is reflected even by small objects.
- **Bats** send out ultrasonic squeaks and locate insects and obstacles from the echoes (echolocation).
- **Dolphins** use ultrasonic clicks to find fish and to navigate in murky water.
- **Fishing boats** use echoes to find shoals of fish.
- **Medical imaging (ultrasonography):** echoes from organs build a picture of the heart, liver, kidneys or a baby in the womb, without harmful radiation.

rows: Image organs and the unborn baby

visual.alt: Table of users of echoes, the sound they use and its purpose

slides.narration: Bats hunt in the dark by sending out very high squeaks that we cannot hear, then listening for the echoes from insects. Dolphins do the same under water. Fishing boats use echoes to find shoals of fish, and doctors use ultrasound echoes to see inside the body safely, for example to check on a baby before it is born.

slides.heading: SONAR: measuring the depth of the sea
slides.body_md:
**SONAR** (Sound Navigation And Ranging) uses a **transmitter** on a ship to send a short pulse of **ultrasound** down into the water and a **receiver** to pick up the echo. The time $t$ between sending and receiving is measured, and with the speed of sound in sea water (about **1500 m/s**):
$$\text{depth} = \frac{v t}{2}$$
SONAR also finds submarines, wrecks, icebergs and shoals of fish. **Ultrasound** is used because it is **not heard**, travels as a **narrow beam** with little spreading, and is not easily absorbed.

slides.narration: A SONAR set on a ship sends a short burst of ultrasound straight down. The pulse reflects from the seabed, or from anything in between such as a shoal of fish, and the receiver picks up the echo. The depth is the speed of sound in sea water, about fifteen hundred metres per second, times the echo time, divided by two.

slides.heading: Worked example: depth of the sea
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A ship’s SONAR receives the echo from the seabed 3.0 s after the pulse is sent. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. (a) Find the depth of the sea. (b) An echo from a submarine arrives after 0.6 s. How deep is the submarine?

**(a)** $\text{depth} = \dfrac{v t}{2} = \dfrac{1500 \times 3.0}{2} = 2250$ m.

**(b)** $\dfrac{1500 \times 0.6}{2} = 450$ m below the ship.

visual.alt: Table of echo times and depths in the SONAR example

slides.narration: The pulse goes down and comes back, so halve the total distance. Fifteen hundred metres per second times three seconds is four thousand five hundred metres, and half of that is two thousand two hundred and fifty metres. For the submarine, fifteen hundred times point six, halved, gives four hundred and fifty metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: SONAR
slides.body_md: Find a depth from a SONAR echo time.
slides.narration: Quick check. Depth is the speed of sound in water times the echo time, divided by two.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Echo: reflected sound heard separately from the original.
Conditions: echo at least 0.1 s later, so reflector at least about 17 m away in air; large reflector; loud sound.
d = v t / 2 and v = 2d / t.
Ultrasound (above 20 kHz) is used by bats, dolphins, fishing boats, doctors and SONAR.
SONAR: depth = v t / 2 with v ≈ 1500 m/s in sea water.

rows: Speed of sound in sea water

visual.alt: Summary table of typical values for echoes

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. An echo is reflected sound heard separately from the original. For that, it must come back at least a tenth of a second later, so the reflector must be about seventeen metres away or more. Distance equals speed times time, divided by two. Ultrasound echoes help bats, dolphins, doctors and ships.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Always divide by 2 for an echo: the sound goes there AND back.
Justify 17 m using 0.1 s and the speed of sound.
Use about 1500 m/s for sea water, not 340 m/s.
Name ultrasound and give a reason (narrow beam, not heard) when explaining SONAR.

rows: Speed in air used for sea water
Any small distance gives an echo
At least about 17 m in air

visual.alt: Table of four common slips about echoes and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. In every echo problem, remember the sound travels there and back, so divide by two. Explain the seventeen metre limit using one tenth of a second. Use about fifteen hundred metres per second for sound in sea water. And when you explain SONAR, say that it uses ultrasound, which travels in a narrow beam.

decks.title: Sound — Part 2: Vibrations, resonance and the characteristics of sound
goals: Distinguish natural, damped and forced vibrations with one example each
Explain resonance using two pendulums on a common string, with useful and harmful examples
Relate loudness to amplitude, pitch to frequency and quality to waveform
Name the decibel and suggest ways to reduce noise pollution

slides.heading: Why does a bridge shake and a flute sing?
slides.body_md: Part 2 — every object has its own way of vibrating. Pushing it at just the right rhythm makes it vibrate hugely; and the way a source vibrates decides how loud, how high and how rich its sound is.

rows: A swing pushed in step goes higher and higher
A struck bell slowly dies away
A tabla and a whistle sound different
A drum hit harder sounds louder

visual.alt: Table of everyday events and the ideas from this part that explain them

slides.narration: Push a child on a swing in step with its swinging, and it goes higher and higher. Strike a bell and its sound slowly dies away. A tabla and a whistle sound different even when equally loud. In this part we look at how things vibrate, at resonance, and at what makes sounds loud or soft, high or low, rich or plain.

slides.heading: Natural and damped vibrations
slides.body_md:
**Natural (free) vibrations:** a body set vibrating and left to itself vibrates at its own **natural frequency**, which depends on its **size, shape, material and tension** (for a pendulum, its length). Ideally the amplitude stays constant.

**Damped vibrations:** in practice, friction and air resistance take away energy, so the **amplitude decreases** with time while the **frequency stays the natural frequency**. Examples: a pendulum swinging in air, a struck tuning fork dying away, a plucked string.

visual.alt: Graph of displacement against time for a damped vibration: the oscillation keeps the same period while its amplitude shrinks along a decaying curve
visual.caption: Damped: same frequency, falling amplitude.

slides.narration: Pull a pendulum aside and let go. It swings at its own natural frequency, which depends on its length. If there were no air or friction, it would keep swinging with the same size of swing. In real life, air resistance steals energy, so the swings get smaller and smaller, while the time for each swing stays the same. These are damped vibrations.

slides.heading: Forced vibrations
slides.body_md: **Forced vibrations:** a body made to vibrate by an **external periodic force** vibrates at the **frequency of that force**, not at its own natural frequency. The amplitude is usually **small**, unless the two frequencies are close. Examples: the stem of a vibrating tuning fork pressed on a table top makes the table vibrate and the sound louder; the sound board of a sitar or guitar is forced to vibrate by the strings; a house window rattles when a heavy truck passes.

rows: Table top pressed by a tuning fork

visual.alt: Table comparing natural, damped and forced vibrations

slides.narration: When an outside force keeps pushing a body back and forth, the body vibrates at the frequency of that force, whatever its own natural frequency. Press the stem of a ringing tuning fork on a table, and the table top is forced to vibrate with it, making the sound louder. The body of a guitar is forced to vibrate by its strings.

slides.heading: Worked example: natural frequency of a swing
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A garden swing completes 20 oscillations in 50 s. (a) Find its natural frequency. (b) At what frequency should a child push it to make it go higher and higher? (c) If an adult instead pushes once every 2 s, what kind of vibration results?

**(a)** $f = \dfrac{\text{oscillations}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{20}{50} = 0.4$ Hz (time period $= \dfrac{1}{0.4} = 2.5$ s).

**(b)** At $0.4$ Hz — once every 2.5 s — in step with the swing (resonance).

**(c)** Pushing at $\dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$ Hz forces the swing at a frequency different from 0.4 Hz: a **forced vibration** with only a small amplitude.

visual.alt: Table of the values in the swing example

slides.narration: Twenty swings in fifty seconds is a frequency of point four hertz, one swing every two and a half seconds. Pushing at exactly that rhythm adds energy at the right moment every time, so the swing goes higher. Pushing every two seconds does not match its natural frequency, so the swing is forced to move but never builds up a large swing.

slides.heading: Quick check: damped vibrations
slides.body_md: Identify what changes in a damped vibration.
slides.narration: Quick check. In damped vibrations, think about which quantity falls with time.

slides.heading: Resonance: two pendulums on a common string
slides.body_md:
**Resonance** is a special case of forced vibration: when the frequency of the applied force **equals the natural frequency** of the body, the body vibrates with a **very large amplitude**.

**Demonstration:** several pendulums hang from a common stretched string. A heavy pendulum D is set swinging; it forces all the others to vibrate through the string. The pendulum **B of the same length** as D (same natural frequency) soon swings with a **large amplitude** — it resonates — while pendulums of other lengths only make small, irregular swings.

slides.narration: Hang several pendulums from one stretched string and set the heavy one swinging. Its pulls travel along the string and push on all the others. Only the pendulum with exactly the same length, and so the same natural frequency, picks up a big swing. The others just jiggle a little. This build up of a large vibration is called resonance.

slides.heading: Resonance: useful and harmful
slides.body_md:
**Useful:** tuning a **radio** to a station (the circuit resonates with the station’s frequency); musical instruments — the **air column** of a flute or the hollow body of a tabla resonates and makes the sound louder; finding the frequency of a tuning fork with a resonance tube.

**Harmful:** soldiers **break step** while crossing a bridge so that their marching cannot set it into resonance; machines are mounted on rubber so their vibrations do not shake buildings; a singer’s steady note at the right pitch can **shatter a glass**; wind gusts set the Tacoma Narrows bridge (USA, 1940) swinging until it collapsed.

visual.alt: Graph of the amplitude of a forced vibration against the ratio of forcing frequency to natural frequency, with a sharp peak at a ratio of one
visual.caption: Largest amplitude when the frequencies match.

slides.narration: The graph shows how big a forced vibration gets. Far from the natural frequency, the amplitude is small; when the frequencies match, it shoots up. Resonance is useful in radios and musical instruments. But it can be dangerous: soldiers break step on bridges, and a steady wind once shook a large bridge until it collapsed.

slides.heading: Quick check: resonance
slides.body_md: Decide when resonance occurs.
slides.narration: Quick check. Resonance needs the forcing frequency to equal the natural frequency.

slides.heading: Loudness and pitch
slides.body_md:
**Loudness** is how strong a sound seems to the ear. It depends on the **amplitude**: loudness (intensity) $\propto (\text{amplitude})^{2}$, so doubling the amplitude makes the intensity four times. It also depends on the **area of the vibrating body**, the **distance** from the source and the **density of the medium**.

**Pitch** is how high or shrill a sound is. It depends on **frequency**: a higher frequency gives a higher (shriller) pitch. A woman’s voice usually has a higher pitch than a man’s; a mosquito’s buzz has a higher pitch than a lion’s roar, though the roar is louder.

visual.alt: Three sound waves showing loud and soft notes of the same pitch, and a note of higher pitch

slides.narration: Loudness depends on amplitude, the size of the vibration. Hit a drum harder and it vibrates more widely, so it sounds louder. Pitch depends on frequency, the number of vibrations each second. A mosquito beats its wings very fast, so its buzz has a high pitch, while a lion’s roar has a low pitch even though it is much louder.

slides.heading: Quality (timbre)
slides.body_md:
**Quality** (timbre) is the characteristic that lets us tell apart two sounds of the **same pitch and loudness**, for example the same note on a sitar and a harmonium, or two friends’ voices on the phone. It depends on the **waveform**, that is, on the **number and relative strengths of the overtones** mixed with the fundamental. A tuning fork gives a pure, sine-shaped wave; instruments give complex waves.

**Subjective and objective:** loudness, pitch and quality are **subjective** (how the listener perceives the sound); the matching **objective**, measurable quantities are **intensity** (W/m²), **frequency** (Hz) and **waveform**.

visual.alt: A pure sine wave from a tuning fork and a wave with overtones from an instrument, same pitch and loudness

slides.narration: Play the same note equally loudly on a sitar and on a harmonium, and you can still tell them apart. That difference is called quality. It comes from the shape of the wave: besides the main note, each instrument gives a mixture of higher overtones. A tuning fork gives a smooth, pure wave; real instruments give richer, more complicated ones.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading a waveform
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A microphone connected to a CRO shows a steady wave whose time period is 2.5 ms. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. (a) Find the frequency. (b) Find the wavelength. (c) The amplitude on the screen is then doubled with the frequency unchanged. What happens to the pitch and to the intensity?

**(a)** $f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{0.0025} = 400$ Hz.

**(b)** $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{340}{400} = 0.85$ m.

**(c)** Pitch is unchanged (same frequency); intensity $\propto$ amplitude², so it becomes $2^{2} = 4$ times.

visual.alt: Table of the values in the waveform example

slides.narration: The frequency is one divided by the time period. Two and a half milliseconds is point zero zero two five seconds, so the frequency is four hundred hertz. The wavelength is speed divided by frequency, three hundred and forty over four hundred, or point eight five metres. Doubling the amplitude leaves the pitch the same but makes the sound four times as intense.

slides.heading: The decibel and noise pollution
slides.body_md:
**Sound level** is measured in **decibels (dB)**. 0 dB is the faintest sound a normal ear can hear; each **increase of 10 dB** means the intensity is **10 times** greater. Prolonged exposure above about **80–85 dB** can damage hearing; about 120 dB causes pain.

**Noise** is unwanted, unpleasant sound. **Noise pollution** causes stress, loss of sleep, high blood pressure and hearing loss. **Reducing it:** silencers on vehicles and machines; banning pressure horns and loud speakers at night; planting **trees** along roads; sound-proofing walls with soft, porous materials; keeping factories and airports away from homes; ear protection for workers.

visual.alt: Table of typical sound levels of four sources in decibels

slides.narration: Sound level is measured in decibels. Zero decibels is the faintest sound we can hear, normal talk is about sixty, and busy traffic is about eighty. Every ten decibels more means ten times the intensity. Long exposure to loud noise damages hearing and causes stress. We can reduce noise with silencers, trees, sound proofing and sensible rules on horns and loudspeakers.

slides.heading: Quick check: pitch
slides.body_md: Decide which characteristic of sound depends on frequency.
slides.narration: Quick check. Pitch is the characteristic linked to the number of vibrations each second.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Natural vibration: at the natural frequency; damped: amplitude falls, frequency unchanged; forced: at the frequency of the applied force.
Resonance: forcing frequency = natural frequency → very large amplitude (Barton’s pendulums).
Useful: radio tuning, instruments; harmful: bridges, machines, glass shattering.
Loudness ∝ amplitude²; pitch depends on frequency; quality depends on waveform (overtones).
Sound level in decibels; noise pollution reduced by silencers, trees, sound-proofing, rules.

visual.alt: Summary table linking the three characteristics of sound to the physical quantities they depend on

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Bodies vibrate freely at their natural frequency, the vibrations die away when damped, and an outside force makes them vibrate at its own frequency. When the two frequencies match, resonance gives a huge amplitude. Loudness depends on amplitude, pitch on frequency and quality on the shape of the wave.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: In damped vibrations the FREQUENCY stays the same; only the amplitude falls.
Define resonance as a special case of forced vibration with equal frequencies.
Do not mix up loudness (amplitude) with pitch (frequency).
For Barton’s pendulums, say WHY the equal-length pendulum resonates: same natural frequency.

visual.alt: Table of four common slips in Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. Damping makes the amplitude fall, but the frequency stays the same. Describe resonance as a forced vibration in which the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency. Keep loudness and pitch apart: loudness goes with amplitude and pitch with frequency. In the pendulum experiment, say that the resonating pendulum has the same length as the driver.

notes.title: Sound — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Reflection of sound and echoes
sections.body_md:
- Sound is reflected by hard, large surfaces and obeys the laws of reflection.
- **Echo:** sound heard after reflection from a distant obstacle, separately from the original sound.
- **Conditions:** (1) the echo must reach the ear at least **0.1 s** after the original sound (persistence of hearing); (2) so the reflector must be at least **17 m** away in air ($340 \times 0.1 \div 2$); (3) the reflector must be large compared with the wavelength; (4) the sound must be loud enough.
- **Echo relations:** $d = \dfrac{v t}{2}$, $v = \dfrac{2d}{t}$, $t = \dfrac{2d}{v}$.
- Between two cliffs, with echoes after $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$: distance between the cliffs $= \dfrac{v (t_{1} + t_{2})}{2}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A sound heard after reflection from a distant obstacle, distinctly after the original sound.
The time, about 0.1 s, for which the sensation of a sound lasts in the ear.

visual.alt: Table of minimum echo distance for three speeds of sound in air

sections.heading: 2. Uses of echoes and SONAR
sections.body_md:
- **Ultrasound:** frequency above 20 kHz; short wavelength, so it travels in a narrow beam with little spreading and is reflected by small objects.
- **Bats** (echolocation), **dolphins**, **fishing boats** (shoals), **medical ultrasonography** (organs, unborn baby; no harmful radiation).
- **SONAR:** transmitter sends an ultrasonic pulse into the sea; receiver detects the echo; $\text{depth} = \dfrac{v t}{2}$ with $v \approx 1500$ m/s in sea water. Also finds submarines, wrecks and icebergs.

key_terms.definition_md: Sound Navigation And Ranging: a method of finding the distance of underwater objects from the echoes of ultrasonic pulses.
Sound of frequency above 20 kHz, beyond the range of human hearing.

visual.alt: Table of SONAR echo times and depths for sound at fifteen hundred metres per second

sections.heading: 3. Natural, damped and forced vibrations
sections.body_md:
- **Natural (free) vibration:** at the body’s own natural frequency, which depends on its size, shape, material, tension (pendulum: length); constant amplitude in the absence of resistance.
- **Damped vibration:** amplitude decreases because of friction and air resistance; frequency stays the natural frequency (pendulum in air, struck tuning fork).
- **Forced vibration:** caused by an external periodic force; the body vibrates at the frequency of the force; amplitude usually small (table top under a tuning fork, sound board of a sitar).

key_terms.definition_md: The frequency at which a body vibrates when it is disturbed and left free.
A vibration whose amplitude decreases with time because of resistive forces.
A vibration produced by an external periodic force, at the frequency of that force.

visual.alt: Table of frequency and amplitude for the three kinds of vibration

sections.heading: 4. Resonance
sections.body_md:
- **Resonance:** a special case of forced vibration in which the frequency of the applied force equals the natural frequency of the body, giving a very large amplitude.
- **Demonstration (Barton’s pendulums):** pendulums on a common string; the heavy driver forces all the others; only the one of equal length (same natural frequency) swings with a large amplitude.
- **Useful:** radio tuning; air columns and hollow bodies of musical instruments; resonance tube.
- **Harmful:** soldiers break step on bridges; machines on rubber mountings; glass shattered by a sung note; Tacoma Narrows bridge collapse (1940).

key_terms.definition_md: The large-amplitude vibration of a body when an applied periodic force has a frequency equal to its natural frequency.

visual.alt: Table comparing ordinary forced vibration with resonance

sections.heading: 5. Characteristics of sound; decibel; noise pollution
sections.body_md:
- **Loudness** (subjective) depends on **amplitude**: intensity $\propto A^{2}$; also on the area of the vibrating body, distance from the source, density of the medium. **Intensity** (objective) is the sound energy per second per unit area, in W m⁻².
- **Pitch** (subjective) depends on **frequency** (objective): higher frequency, shriller sound.
- **Quality / timbre** (subjective) depends on the **waveform**, set by the number and relative strengths of overtones; lets us tell sources apart at equal pitch and loudness.
- **Decibel (dB):** unit of sound level; +10 dB means 10 times the intensity; above about 80–85 dB is harmful over long periods.
- **Noise pollution:** unwanted loud sound; causes stress, sleeplessness, hearing loss; reduce with silencers, trees, sound-proofing, rules on horns and loudspeakers.

key_terms.definition_md: The characteristic of sound by which a shrill note is distinguished from a flat one; it depends on frequency.
The characteristic that distinguishes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness; it depends on the waveform.
The unit used to express the level of a sound.

visual.alt: Table of characteristics of sound, what each depends on and whether it is subjective or objective

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Forgetting to halve the round-trip distance in echo and SONAR problems.
- Using 340 m/s for sound in sea water.
- Saying damping lowers the frequency.
- Confusing loudness with pitch.
- Calling every forced vibration “resonance”.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Echo numericals: formula d = vt/2 (1), substitution (1), answer with unit (1).
- Resonance: definition with “equal frequency” (1), demonstration (1), example (1).
- Characteristics: each characteristic with the quantity it depends on (1 each).

questions.stem_md: On a cold winter morning sound travels at 330 m/s in air. The least distance of a hillside from a shepherd, for him to hear a distinct echo of his whistle, is:
Kavya shouts towards a hill 255 m away. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, she hears the echo after:
Clapping in a small classroom 6 m long does not produce a distinct echo because:

options.text_md: the reflected sound returns in less than 0.1 s and merges with the original sound
sound is not reflected by classroom walls
sound travels faster in a closed room
the walls absorb all the sound

questions.solution_md: The round trip of 12 m takes about 0.035 s, less than the persistence of hearing — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A strong, distinct echo is most likely to be heard from:

options.text_md: a large brick wall 5 m away
a large, hard rock face about 50 m away

questions.solution_md: The reflector must be large, hard and at least about 17 m away — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A boy fires a cracker 165 m from a tall wall and hears the echo exactly 1.0 s later. Find the speed of sound in m/s.
A trekker standing between two parallel cliffs claps once. She hears the first echo after 0.8 s and the second after 1.4 s. If sound travels at 340 m/s, how far apart are the cliffs, in metres?
A starter’s pistol is fired 510 m from the wall of a stadium stand. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, after how many seconds is the echo heard at the pistol?

Standing 100 m from a long wall, Ishita claps steadily so that each echo coincides with her next clap. She counts 100 claps in one minute. Find the speed of sound in m/s, to three significant figures.
questions.solution_md: Time between claps $= \dfrac{60}{100} = 0.6$ s, which is the echo time. $v = \dfrac{2d}{t} = \dfrac{2 \times 100}{0.6} = 333.3$ m/s, about 333 m/s.

questions.stem_md: True or false? With sound travelling at 340 m/s in air, a distinct echo can be heard from a wall only 10 m away.
questions.solution_md: False: the round trip of 20 m takes about 0.06 s, less than 0.1 s; the wall must be at least about 17 m away.

questions.stem_md: The sensation of a sound persists in the human ear for about ___ second.

**Assertion (A):** No distinct echo of a shout is heard from a wall 8 m away in air.

**Reason (R):** The reflected sound returns in less than 0.1 s and merges with the original.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true (round trip 16 m takes about 0.047 s), and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a long stone temple corridor, Meera claps once and hears the clap again a moment later. Name this returned sound and the effect that produces it.

answer.model_answer_md: An echo, produced by the reflection of sound from a distant hard surface.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a person must stand at least about 17 m from a reflecting wall to hear a distinct echo in air (speed of sound 340 m/s).

answer.model_answer_md: The ear retains a sound for about 0.1 s, so the echo must arrive at least 0.1 s after the original. In 0.1 s sound travels 340 × 0.1 = 34 m; this is the distance to the wall and back, so the wall must be at least 17 m away.

marking_scheme.step: 34 m there and back, so 17 m

questions.stem_md: A girl standing 25 m from a high wall bursts a balloon and hears the echo 0.15 s later. (a) Calculate the speed of sound. (b) Was the echo distinct? Give a reason. (c) If she moves to 15 m from the wall, after what time would the echo return, and would it be distinct?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $v = \dfrac{2 \times 25}{0.15} = 333$ m/s. (b) Yes: 0.15 s is more than 0.1 s. (c) $t = \dfrac{2 \times 15}{333} \approx 0.09$ s, less than 0.1 s, so the echo would merge with the original sound and not be distinct.

questions.stem_md: A survey ship’s SONAR receives the echo from the seabed 2.0 s after sending the pulse. With sound travelling at 1500 m/s in sea water, the depth of the sea is:
SONAR uses ultrasound rather than audible sound mainly because ultrasound:

options.text_md: travels much faster than audible sound in water
travels as a narrow beam with little spreading and is reflected even by small objects
is not reflected by the seabed

questions.solution_md: Short wavelength gives a narrow, well-directed beam — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A bat flies through a dark cave without hitting the walls because it:

options.text_md: sees the walls with very sensitive eyes
feels the walls with its wings
follows the warmth of the rocks
sends out ultrasonic squeaks and judges distances from their echoes

questions.solution_md: Bats use echolocation with ultrasound — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Doctors examine an unborn baby with ultrasound rather than X-rays because ultrasound:

options.text_md: forms images from echoes without harmful radiation
passes through bones more easily than X-rays

questions.solution_md: Ultrasound echoes give images safely — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A diving team uses SONAR to find an old shipwreck. The echo from the wreck returns 0.8 s after the pulse is sent. Taking the speed of sound in sea water as 1500 m/s, how deep is the wreck in metres?
A dolphin sends out a click and hears its echo from a fish 0.08 s later. If sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water, how far away is the fish in metres?
A bat is 1.7 m from a moth. Its ultrasonic squeak travels at 340 m/s. After how many milliseconds does the echo reach the bat?
Sound of frequency higher than 20 kHz, which humans cannot hear, is called ___.
True or false? SONAR finds the depth of the sea from the time taken by light to travel to the seabed and back.
questions.solution_md: False: it uses the echo time of ultrasonic sound.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Fishing trawlers use ultrasonic pulses to locate shoals of fish.

**Reason (R):** Ultrasound has a short wavelength, so it travels as a narrow beam and is reflected even by small objects.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Explain how a ship’s SONAR measures the depth of the sea below it.

answer.model_answer_md: A transmitter on the ship sends a short pulse of ultrasound down to the seabed, and a receiver picks up the reflected pulse (echo). The time t between sending and receiving is measured; since the pulse goes down and back, depth = v t ÷ 2, where v (about 1500 m/s) is the speed of sound in sea water.

marking_scheme.step: Pulse and echo detected, time measured

questions.stem_md: Give two uses of echoes made by animals and two made by people.

answer.model_answer_md: Animals: bats locate insects and obstacles; dolphins find fish and navigate. People: SONAR on ships finds sea depth, wrecks and shoals of fish; doctors make ultrasound scans of organs and unborn babies.

questions.stem_md: A simple pendulum is left swinging in a room. After a few minutes:

options.text_md: its frequency has decreased, but its amplitude is the same
its amplitude has decreased, but its frequency is the same
both its amplitude and frequency have increased
its amplitude is unchanged and it swings faster

questions.solution_md: Air resistance damps the motion: amplitude falls, natural frequency is unchanged — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The stem of a vibrating tuning fork is pressed against a wooden table top and the sound becomes louder. This is because:

options.text_md: the tuning fork vibrates with a higher frequency
the table top is made to vibrate (forced vibration), and its large area sets more air vibrating
the table top vibrates at its own natural frequency only

questions.solution_md: The table vibrates at the fork’s frequency as a forced vibration; a large vibrating area gives a louder sound — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The natural frequency of a simple pendulum can be changed by changing its:
questions.solution_md: The natural frequency of a pendulum depends on its length — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A pendulum in a wall clock makes 30 complete oscillations in 24 s. Find its natural frequency in Hz.
True or false? In damped vibrations, the frequency of the vibrating body gradually decreases.
questions.solution_md: False: the amplitude decreases; the frequency stays the natural frequency.

questions.stem_md: A body made to vibrate by an external periodic force vibrates with the ___ of that force.

**Assertion (A):** The sound of a temple bell slowly dies away after it is struck.

**Reason (R):** The vibrations of the bell are damped by air resistance and internal friction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between natural vibrations and forced vibrations, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Natural vibrations take place at the body’s own natural frequency when it is disturbed and left free (a pendulum pulled aside and released). Forced vibrations take place at the frequency of an external periodic force acting on the body (the sound board of a sitar vibrating with its strings).

questions.stem_md: Classify each as natural, damped or forced vibration: (a) a guitar string plucked and allowed to ring until silent, (b) a window pane rattling while a heavy truck passes, (c) an ideal pendulum swinging in a vacuum with no friction.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Damped: the amplitude falls as energy is lost to the air and the body of the guitar. (b) Forced: the pane vibrates at the frequency of the truck’s vibrations. (c) Natural: it swings at its natural frequency with constant amplitude.

questions.stem_md: A body is set into vibration by a periodic force. It vibrates with the largest amplitude when the frequency of the force is:

options.text_md: twice the natural frequency of the body
much less than the natural frequency of the body
equal to the natural frequency of the body
much greater than the natural frequency of the body

questions.stem_md: Pendulums of lengths 40 cm, 60 cm, 80 cm and 100 cm hang from a common string. A heavy driver pendulum of length 60 cm is set swinging. The pendulum that swings with the largest amplitude is the one of length:
questions.solution_md: Equal length gives equal natural frequency, so the 60 cm pendulum resonates — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Soldiers marching across a suspension bridge are ordered to break step because:

options.text_md: marching in step makes too much noise
their regular steps could match the natural frequency of the bridge and make it vibrate dangerously
the bridge is weaker in the middle
marching in step increases their weight

questions.stem_md: Turning the tuning knob of a radio to pick up one particular station is an example of:
questions.solution_md: The circuit’s natural frequency is matched to the station’s frequency — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Resonance is a special case of forced vibration.
questions.solution_md: True: it is forced vibration at a frequency equal to the natural frequency.

questions.stem_md: When the frequency of the applied force equals the natural frequency of a body and the body vibrates with a large amplitude, the effect is called ___.

**Assertion (A):** A pendulum of length 50 cm hanging from a common string resonates with a driver pendulum of length 80 cm.

**Reason (R):** Resonance occurs only when the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is false — different lengths give different natural frequencies; R is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A trained singer holding one steady note can make a thin wine glass shatter.

**Reason (R):** When the frequency of the note equals the natural frequency of the glass, its vibrations build up to a very large amplitude.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give one example where resonance is useful and one where it must be avoided, explaining each briefly.

answer.model_answer_md: Useful: tuning a radio, where the circuit is adjusted until its natural frequency matches that of the station, so that station’s signal is strongly received. Avoided: soldiers break step on a bridge, so that their steps cannot match the bridge’s natural frequency and build up dangerous vibrations.

questions.stem_md: Describe an experiment with pendulums hung from a common string to demonstrate resonance, and state what is observed and why.

answer.model_answer_md: Hang several light pendulums of different lengths and one heavy driver pendulum from a horizontal string stretched between two supports, with one light pendulum of the same length as the driver. Set the driver swinging at right angles to the string. All the pendulums start to swing, but the one of equal length soon swings with a large amplitude, while the others swing only slightly. It has the same natural frequency as the driver, so it is in resonance.

questions.stem_md: The shrillness of the whistle of a pressure cooker compared with the hum of a refrigerator is described by its:
The amplitude of vibration of a loudspeaker cone is doubled at the same frequency. The intensity of the sound becomes:

options.text_md: unchanged, because the frequency is the same

questions.solution_md: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared: $2^{2} = 4$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: You recognise your friend’s voice on the phone even before she says her name. The characteristic of sound that makes this possible is its:
questions.solution_md: Each voice has its own waveform (overtones) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Compared with the roar of a lion, the buzz of a mosquito has:

options.text_md: a higher pitch but a much smaller loudness
a lower pitch and a smaller loudness
a higher pitch and a greater loudness
the same pitch but a different quality

questions.solution_md: The mosquito’s wings vibrate at high frequency with small amplitude — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which pair consists of objective (measurable) quantities rather than subjective sensations?
questions.solution_md: Loudness, pitch and quality depend on the listener; intensity and frequency are measured — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A sound-level meter near a busy crossing reads 80. The unit of this reading is the:
questions.solution_md: Sound level is measured in decibels — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A tuning fork of frequency 512 Hz sounds in air where sound travels at 340 m/s. Find the wavelength of the sound in metres, to three significant figures.
The sound of a ship’s horn has a wavelength of 1.36 m in air (speed of sound 340 m/s). Find its frequency in Hz.
The amplitude of vibration of a drum skin is made three times as large, with the frequency unchanged. By what factor does the intensity of its sound increase?
Normal conversation is about 60 dB and busy traffic about 80 dB. Using the fact that each increase of 10 dB means ten times the intensity, how many times more intense is the traffic noise?
questions.solution_md: An increase of $80 - 60 = 20$ dB is two steps of 10 dB, so the factor is $10 \times 10 = 100$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A louder sound always has a higher pitch.
questions.solution_md: False: loudness depends on amplitude, pitch on frequency; they are independent.

questions.stem_md: The pitch of a sound depends on its ___.
The level of a sound, as shown on a sound-level meter, is expressed in ___.

**Assertion (A):** A flute and a violin playing the same note equally loudly can still be told apart.

**Reason (R):** The two instruments produce sound waves of different waveforms, with different overtones.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Striking a tabla harder makes its sound louder.

**Reason (R):** The pitch of a sound depends on the amplitude of vibration.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true (larger amplitude); R is false — pitch depends on frequency — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Apart from amplitude, name one factor on which the loudness of a sound depends.

answer.model_answer_md: The area of the vibrating body (also the distance from the source or the density of the medium).

questions.stem_md: A housing colony is built beside a busy highway. Suggest two ways to reduce the noise reaching the homes, and state one harmful effect of long exposure to such noise.

answer.model_answer_md: Plant thick rows of trees or build a sound barrier wall along the highway; fit double-glazed windows and sound-absorbing curtains (also enforce silencers and limits on horns). Long exposure can cause hearing loss, stress, sleeplessness or high blood pressure.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by saying that loudness is a subjective quantity while intensity is objective? Name the objective quantity that corresponds to pitch.

answer.model_answer_md: Loudness is the sensation produced in a listener’s ear, so it differs from person to person; intensity is the measurable sound energy per second per unit area, the same for every observer. The objective quantity matching pitch is frequency.

questions.stem_md: Match each characteristic or quantity of sound in Column A with what it depends on, or its unit, in Column B.
questions.solution_md: Loudness → amplitude; pitch → frequency; quality → waveform; sound level → decibel.

questions.stem_md: For each sound or vibration event in Column A, pick the physics behind it from Column B.

options.text_md: A ship finds the depth of the sea
A struck bell slowly falls silent
A table top hums when a vibrating fork is pressed on it
An equal-length pendulum picks up a large swing

questions.solution_md: Sea depth → echo of ultrasound; bell → damped; table top → forced; equal-length pendulum → resonance.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is an echo? State two conditions necessary for hearing a distinct echo. [3]

(b) Show that the minimum distance of a reflector for a distinct echo in air is about 17 m, taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s. [3]

(c) A man stands between two buildings and fires a gun. He hears the first echo after 1.2 s and the second after 2.5 s. (i) How far is each building from him? (ii) How far apart are the buildings? (iii) When will he hear a third echo, from sound reflected by both buildings? (speed of sound 340 m/s) [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An echo is a sound heard after reflection from a distant obstacle, separately from the original sound. Conditions: the echo must reach the ear at least 0.1 s after the original (so the reflector is at least about 17 m away); the reflector must be large compared with the wavelength (and the sound must be loud enough).

(b) The ear retains a sound for 0.1 s. In 0.1 s sound travels $340 \times 0.1 = 34$ m, there and back, so the minimum distance is $\dfrac{34}{2} = 17$ m.

(c) (i) $\dfrac{340 \times 1.2}{2} = 204$ m and $\dfrac{340 \times 2.5}{2} = 425$ m. (ii) $204 + 425 = 629$ m. (iii) The sound reflected first by one building then the other travels twice the gap: $t = 1.2 + 2.5 = 3.7$ s.

questions.solution_md: Definition and conditions; 17 m; two distances, gap, third echo.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is ultrasound? Give two reasons why it is used in SONAR. [3]

(b) Describe, with the help of a labelled sketch described in words, how SONAR is used to find the depth of the sea. [3]

(c) A ship’s SONAR receives an echo from the seabed 4.0 s after sending a pulse. (i) Find the depth of the sea. (ii) A submarine lies 450 m below the ship; after what time does its echo arrive? (iii) Why is 340 m/s not used here? (speed of sound in sea water 1500 m/s) [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Ultrasound is sound of frequency above 20 kHz. It is used because it travels in a narrow beam with little spreading (short wavelength), it is reflected even by small objects, and it cannot be heard, so it does not disturb people.

(b) A transmitter fixed under the ship sends a short ultrasonic pulse downwards; it is reflected by the seabed and the echo is picked up by a receiver beside the transmitter. The time interval t is measured, and depth = v t ÷ 2.

(c) (i) $\dfrac{1500 \times 4.0}{2} = 3000$ m. (ii) $t = \dfrac{2 \times 450}{1500} = 0.6$ s. (iii) 340 m/s is the speed of sound in air; sound travels much faster in water.

questions.solution_md: Ultrasound and reasons; SONAR method; depth, time, speed in water.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define natural, damped and forced vibrations. [3]

(b) A pendulum swinging in air is observed for a few minutes. Describe how its displacement–time graph changes with time, and state what happens to (i) its amplitude and (ii) its frequency. [3]

(c) (i) What is resonance? (ii) Describe how two pendulums of equal length on a common string show resonance. (iii) Why does a pendulum of a different length not resonate? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Natural vibrations: vibrations of a body at its own natural frequency when disturbed and left free. Damped vibrations: vibrations whose amplitude decreases with time because of resistive forces. Forced vibrations: vibrations of a body under an external periodic force, at the frequency of that force.

(b) The graph is a wave of constant period whose peaks shrink steadily along a decaying envelope. (i) The amplitude decreases. (ii) The frequency stays the same (the natural frequency).

(c) (i) Resonance: a forced vibration in which the frequency of the applied force equals the natural frequency of the body, so the amplitude becomes very large. (ii) When one pendulum is set swinging, its pulls on the common string force the other; having the same length, the second has the same natural frequency and soon swings with a large amplitude. (iii) Its natural frequency differs from the driver’s, so it makes only small forced vibrations.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; damped graph; resonance with pendulums.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the difference between forced vibration and resonance. [3]

(b) Give two examples where resonance is useful and one where it is harmful. [3]

(c) A swing completes 12 oscillations in 30 s. (i) Find its natural frequency and time period. (ii) A child pushes it once every 2.5 s. Will its amplitude build up? Explain. (iii) What happens if the child pushes once every 1.5 s instead? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In forced vibration the applied force may have any frequency and the amplitude is usually small; in resonance the applied frequency equals the natural frequency of the body and the amplitude becomes very large.

(b) Useful: tuning a radio; the air column of a flute or the hollow body of a tabla making the sound louder. Harmful: a marching troop setting a bridge into large vibrations (so soldiers break step).

(c) (i) $f = \dfrac{12}{30} = 0.4$ Hz; $T = \dfrac{1}{0.4} = 2.5$ s. (ii) Yes: pushing every 2.5 s is at 0.4 Hz, equal to the natural frequency — resonance. (iii) Pushing at about 0.67 Hz does not match the natural frequency, so the swing makes only small, irregular forced vibrations.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the three characteristics of a musical sound and state the physical quantity on which each depends. [3]

(b) A CRO shows the waveform of a note with a time period of 4.0 ms. (i) Find its frequency. (ii) Find its wavelength in air (speed of sound 340 m/s). (iii) If the amplitude of the waveform is halved at the same frequency, what happens to the intensity? [3]

(c) (i) In what unit is sound level measured? (ii) Why is continuous noise above about 85 dB harmful? (iii) Suggest two ways to reduce noise pollution near a school. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Loudness depends on amplitude (intensity); pitch depends on frequency; quality (timbre) depends on the waveform, that is, the overtones present.

(b) (i) $f = \dfrac{1}{0.004} = 250$ Hz. (ii) $\lambda = \dfrac{340}{250} = 1.36$ m. (iii) Intensity $\propto$ amplitude², so it becomes $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = 0.25$ of its value, one quarter.

(c) (i) The decibel (dB). (ii) It can damage the ear and cause hearing loss, stress and sleeplessness. (iii) Plant trees around the school; ban loud horns and loudspeakers nearby (also sound-proof classrooms).
